newsitem.title: UK: Dollar on a roll in Europe, all eyes on U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar on a roll in Europe, all eyes on U.S. data.

text.p: The dollar continued its winning streak in European trade on Tuesday, with hopes of strong U.S. data and apparent lack of central bank action pushing it to new highs against major currencies.

After the dollar pushed to a 31-month peak of 1.6565 marks and a 47-month high of 120.58 yen, analysts said a strong showing in the fourth-quarter U.S. employment cost index -- considered one of this week's highlights for the market -- could take it even higher.

"People are speculating that perhaps we'll get strong data today and that's helping the dollar as well... as that could raise the chances of an early Fed rate hike," said Thomas Rayner, international economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
By Europe's mid-morning the dollar had subsided to 1.6538 marks and 120.51 yen, although this was around one pfenning and one yen above where it was in late European trade on Monday.

"If we get the employment cost index reported above one percent, we will have good cause for concern and the market will take the dollar higher," said PaineWebber chief international economist Michael O'Hanlon.
A Reuters poll of economists showed the employment cost index for the fourth quarter of 1996, due at 1330 GMT, was on average expected to rise 0.9 percent after a 0.6 percent increase previously.

The market considered the employment cost data a key influence on the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee's decision on interest rates at its meeting next week, especially as Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan last week sounded a warning on the risks of wage-driven inflation in his testimony to the U.S. Senate Budget Committee.
More ammunition for the dollar came from reports that neither Germany nor Japan appeared worried about the dollar's strength against their currencies.
"They (the Japanese authorities) don't see it as a major problem because they see it as a case of a strong dollar rather than a weak yen," Rayner said.

When the dollar hit its high against the yen earlier on Tuesday, a senior official at the Japanese finance ministry was quoted by a domestic news agency as saying that the yen's recent slide against the dollar was not a cause for immediate concern.

Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, meanwhile, told the Handelsblatt newspaper that the German central bank saw no grave risks for price developments despite the dollar's recent surge against the mark.
The market also gained the courage to try for higher levels, particularly against the yen, from the perception that central banks were not selling dollars to rein in the currency.

"The lack of central bank intervention, particularly on the part of the Bank of Japan, is giving the market the temptation to take the dollar higher until we see some sort of official response from the Japanese authorities," PaineWebber's O'Hanlon said.
The dollar also touched a 33-month high of 1.4370 Swiss francs. It had retreated to 1.4325 by mid-morning but was still well above Monday's late European level of 1.4240.
The Swiss franc was unsettled overnight by a media report that Swiss Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger had said he was "relieved" at the currency's recent decline.
